Chapter 2: The Nazi Invasion and the Collapse of Normal Life
When the war finally hit, it wasn’t just one massive blow—it was more like a series of shocks, each one chipping away at the world the Żabińskis had worked so hard to create. September 1939, the German invasion of Poland, turned Warsaw upside down. And the zoo? It was caught right in the middle of the chaos. Bombs rained down, breaking open animal enclosures and sending terrified creatures out into the city streets. The keepers did everything they could to rescue the animals, but many didn’t make it. Some were killed in the blasts, while others were hunted down—either by soldiers or desperate people just trying to survive.
The villa that used to be filled with warmth and laughter became a safe haven against all that violence. Antonina and Jan did their best to comfort their son and care for the animals that survived, but that old feeling of safety? It was gone. Everywhere they looked, the city was different. Streets they once strolled became battle zones, neighbors vanished without a trace, and the old rules of daily life simply stopped mattering. Even the zoo itself was transformed. Any animals that survived the first wave of destruction were often taken by the Germans—sometimes for private collections, sometimes as trophies. The empty cages and silent enclosures were a haunting reminder of all that had been lost.
But even in all this devastation, the Żabińskis faced some tough decisions. The zoo’s official purpose was gone, but their villa and its grounds were still there. Jan, always thinking on his feet, found work with the city’s parks department, which let him move more freely around Warsaw. Meanwhile, Antonina did everything she could to create a sense of normal life for her family, even as things outside grew more dangerous by the day. She filled their home with music and stories, and cared for the animals that were left. Eventually, the villa wasn’t just their home—it became a place where friends, colleagues, and even strangers looking for help could gather.
The Nazi occupation brought new dangers and moral crossroads. The Germans set harsh rules, especially targeting Jews and anyone they considered undesirable. That’s when the Warsaw Ghetto was created, forcing the city’s Jewish population into packed and unsanitary conditions. Rumors about terrible things happening started to spread, and like so many others, the Żabińskis struggled to make sense of the horror all around them. It became clear that the old ways—trusting the law, leaning on institutions—just didn’t offer any protection anymore. Now, survival meant thinking fast, being brave, and being willing to risk everything for someone else.
As time went on, the villa’s role as a safe haven grew even more important. The Żabińskis began to hide not just animals, but people—offering food, shelter, and a little comfort to those running from the Nazis. The skills they’d developed as zookeepers—being observant, patient, and deeply empathetic—suddenly mattered more than ever. They learned to spot fear and desperation, to offer reassurance without attracting attention, and to create a feeling of safety right in the heart of chaos.
Who would have thought a zoo could become a lifeline? But for the people who found shelter there, it truly was—a beacon of hope in one of the darkest times imaginable.
